newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy govt hits 1996 CPI target, optimistic for 97.
newsitem.headline: Italy govt hits 1996 CPI target, optimistic for 97.

text.p: Italian inflation remained steady in December after a year of steep falls and should dip again later in 1997 after an upward blip in January, economists said on Wednesday.

National statistics office Istat said the inflation rate was 2.6 percent year-on-year last month, unchanged from the November level and in line with forecasts. On a month-on-month basis, prices climbed 0.1 percent in December.
This meant average annual inflation in 1996 was 3.9 percent against 5.4 percent in 1995, meeting the government target.
"The 1997 objective of average annual inflation of 2.5 percent is now within reach," the Treasury said in a statement.

Analysts agreed that 2.5 percent was an attainable goal in the face of a subdued economy and weak domestic demand as long as the government did not decide to hike value added tax in its efforts to prepare the economy for the single European currency.
"Ministers might decide that a small rise in inflation is worth the price of getting the deficit in shape for Europe," said Claudio Tosato, economist with Deutsche Bank in Milan.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi and the Bank of Italy have put the battle against inflation at the top of their agendas, seeing this as the key to lasting low interest rates.

The struggle, which involved the central bank keeping its monetary policy extremely tight for much of last year, paid off as inflation tumbled from 5.8 percent in December 1995 to 2.6 percent a year later.
But the downward trend is likely to be interrupted in January for statistical reasons, Istat said.

Istat introduced a new basket of goods to weigh price changes at the start of 1996 and this month will be the first time the year-on-year rate will be compared to the current basket, resulting in a slight increase in the index, an official said.
Ilaria Fornari, economist with bank JP Morgan in Milan, said the inflation rate might climb to 2.7 or 2.8 percent in January.
"But things should improve thereafter, especially in the second quarter as the business cycle continues to deliver disinflation," she said.

Italians' unwillingness to spend money in the current economic climate, where growth is sluggish and taxes are high, has forced businesses to cut their profit margins rather than pass on price rises to clients.
Many people are likely to have more spending money later this year when the long-running wage dispute in the important metalworkers' sector is finally resolved.
Recent pay accords in other sectors have come in around the five percent level and the Bank of Italy has warned that a generous settlement for metalworkers could fuel inflation.
But some analysts doubted whether this would be the case, saying the main threat to prices came from the government.

A large overshoot in 1996's public sector deficit means the government will almost certainly have to introduce a mini-budget in the first half of this year to try to keep alive its hopes of being a founder member of the planned euro currency.
Prodi has said that if a budget is needed it will be based on spending cuts, but a revision of VAT bands might also be needed to bring in a guaranteed level of funds, analysts said.
"This would have a knock-on effect on prices, but if the inflation rate rose to 2.8 or 2.9 percent that would still be inside the terms of the Maastricht treaty," Tosato said.
